transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Argentum Head of Platform), Leah Kim (Argentum Cloud Architect), Omar Hassan (Argentum Sec Eng), Nina Flores (Argentum PM)

Summary: Quick technical sync to align on marketplace onramp, LLM routing policies, and SLA harmonization for Argentum's hybrid product. Discussed fallback policies, VPC/private listing constraints, telemetry/observability hooks, and an initial plan for a short benchmarking pilot.

Topics: marketplace packaging, VPC onramp, model routing (edge vs central), caching/kv tradeoffs, SLA tiers and canary rollouts, KMS/encryption, telemetry and billing tags

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone thanks for hopping on, I think we have about an hour so we'll run through the onramp checklist, your routing needs and then surface any blockers. can everyone hear me?
[00:07] Ravi Patel: yes loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:09] Leah Kim: same here.
[00:11] Diego Alvarez: good afternoon all, diego here, i'll tee up the perf bits after the intro.

[00:20] Maya Chen: quick context, Argentum wants to list a hybrid offering in the Redwood marketplace but with a VPC onramp and some on‑prem connectors. main asks today: 1) how routing and fallbacks work across hosted/dedicated/private, 2) what SLA tiers we can hit with your expected traffic and 3) KMS/audit integration questions. is that still accurate?
[00:36] Nina Flores: that's perfect, and to add — we have regulatory constraints in eu and apac for certain datasets, so region pinning matters.

[00:44] Leah Kim: also cost is a hard constraint at scale, we need to know tradeoffs: low latency 5–20ms vs cheaper batch profiles.

[00:52] Maya Chen: totally. ok diego, can you briefly summarize the runtime options and routing primitives?
[00:56] Diego Alvarez: sure. so Redwood's runtime supports three deployment modes — hosted API, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) and the Private onramp which is the VPC/air‑gapped option. routing policies can be set by region, cost tier, latency SLO or model compatibility. you can declare a policy like: prefer-hosted-if-latency<50ms else route-to-dedicated else fallback-to-quantized-variant. our routing controller will look at model variant compatibility (quantized vs full fp16) and KV cache availability to avoid cold starts.
[01:27] Ravi Patel: when you say KV cache — is that prefix/KV cache that lives in the runtime or something that we need to manage in our infra?
[01:33] Diego Alvarez: good q — it's runtime-managed, but for Private deployments there's an optional external cache hook if you want to pin cache to your redis / memcached to keep data inside your VPC. we can map cache tenancy either to customer‑scoped keyspaces or to instance level.
[01:50] Omar Hassan: that external hook — what about encryption in transit for the cache and at‑rest? our security team needs KMS/HSM integration.
[01:58] Priya Rao: we support TLS mTLS between runtime and external cache, and for at‑rest encryption we integrate with customer KMS providers — aws kms, azure key vault, and common HSM providers. auditing for key rotations is logged to the audit stream.
[02:12] Omar Hassan: ok please push the KMS doc after this call.

[02:17] Maya Chen: we'll do. on the marketplace listing side, there are a couple of packaging options: private listing (visible only to you), marketplace‑public listing, and a hybrid where the control plane is Redwood hosted but the runtime is deployed in your VPC. which model are you targeting?
[02:33] Leah Kim: we want the hybrid: control plane Redwood, runtime in our VPC. we also want the ability to opt into Redwood Dedicated for burst periods.

[02:41] Diego Alvarez: that should work. the hybrid onramp requires a connector that opens egress to Redwood control plane (port 443) and a trust bundle for the control plane to trigger deploys. there is a packaging checklist — includes helm chart, image repo, and a manifest with model variants and attestations.
[02:57] Nina Flores: how long does it usually take to be listed? we have a product deadline late September.
[03:03] Maya Chen: typical onramp is 2–4 weeks if you have a staging cluster and the manifest ready. if we need deeper KMS/HSM validation or SOC‑type audits, that can add time.

[03:12] Ravi Patel: we definitely need SOC2 artifacts. Omar, can you describe the compliance gating?
[03:18] Omar Hassan: sure — primary asks: (1) SOC2 or ISO attestation, (2) audit logs forwarded to our SIEM or to S3 with signed timestamps, (3) KMS integration, (4) RBAC and SSO/SCIM integration for Ops.
[03:31] Priya Rao: we have a SOC2 package — i'll send the redacted attestation. audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via our logging connector or delivered to your S3 with integrity checks. SSO/SCIM is supported; RBAC maps to roles in the control plane.

[03:45] Diego Alvarez: want to bring the conversation back to SLAs: what are the concrete targets? nina, do you have an expected p95/p99 for inference time?
[03:52] Nina Flores: we were hoping for p95 <= 120ms across EU regions for the small‑/medium prompts and p50 <= 40ms. p99 for some heavy queries could be relaxed to 500ms.
[04:03] Diego Alvarez: ok that aligns with Redwood Dedicated in most configs. if you want p95 120ms with consistent tail and regional residency, recommended config is Dedicated in eu-west plus local VPC runtime for sensitive data. quantized variants can help reduce cost but may add 5–15ms decode overhead depending on kernel. also continuous batching will influence tail — so if you want low p50 and controlled p99 you may want to disable large batching for low‑latency routes.
[04:29] Leah Kim: do we get per-route cost estimation? we want to budget per‑million tokens and see billing tags per customer.
[04:35] Maya Chen: yes, console provides token-level cost breakdowns by route/model variant and you can attach billing tags for each route. we'll share an example billing export.

[04:44] Ravi Patel: earlier you mentioned fallback to quantized variants — how graceful is the quality regression and can we set thresholds for automatic rollback?
[04:52] Diego Alvarez: we have a rollback policy tied to evals: you can provide a prompt set and quality metric (exact match, rouge, or custom heuristic). if the fallback variant causes a >X% delta in quality for the eval set, the router will stop sending traffic to that variant and will instead route to the next available candidate. you control thresholds.
[05:11] Nina Flores: do we need to run our evals inside Redwood or can we keep eval data in our environment?
[05:16] Priya Rao: evals can be run client side and you can upload anonymized metrics, or we can run the harness in your staging if you want Redwood to manage evals. many enterprise customers run eval locally for privacy.

[05:28] Omar Hassan: about telemetry — does the runtime expose trace IDs we can connect to our distributed tracing? we need end‑to‑end request IDs.
[05:36] Diego Alvarez: yes, we emit trace IDs and can attach per-token latency breakdowns. we also support OpenTelemetry exporters so you can ingest into Jaeger/Zipkin or your APM — with PII redaction options.

[05:49] Leah Kim: one practical question: if our control plane is Redwood hosted but runtime in our VPC, who owns autoscaling? can Redwood autoscale the runtime or do we have to run a KEDA/HPA solution?
[05:59] Priya Rao: the runtime includes an autoscaler operator that can be run in your cluster. it's declarative — you set policy (min/max GPUs, latency SLOs, cost cap) and the operator will manage scale. for Dedicated we can manage autoscaling remotely if you opt into the managed operations add‑on.

[06:16] Ravi Patel: hmm managed ops might be useful for our first few months. what's the cost premium?
[06:21] Maya Chen: usually a percentage over reserved capacity; i'll include typical numbers in the pricing sheet.

[06:27] Diego Alvarez: quick note about cold starts — large models with big KV caches can have cold startup overhead. our suggestion: warmup hooks and a tiny persistent pool sized to your baseline qps. that avoids tail blips during traffic spikes.

[06:41] Nina Flores: is warmup something we control? we don't want extra idle costs.
[06:46] Diego Alvarez: yes it's policy controlled. you can specify warmup windows or use predictive autoscaling based on historical traces. predictive scaling is a bit more aggressive cost wise but reduces tail events.

[06:58] Leah Kim: we plan to have two classes of traffic: conversational chat (short prompts, high qps) and document summarization (long prompts, lower qps). how would you recommend model variants?
[07:08] Diego Alvarez: conversational: smaller quantized low-latency variant pinned to eu regions. summarization: larger fp16 or bf16 variant on Dedicated or VPC runtime; for cost saving you can run summarization batch jobs with longer token windows on Dedicated cheaper instances. route by path or route header.

[07:27] Ravi Patel: we also want to enable canary rollouts for model updates and have automatic fallback in case the new model increases latency beyond 20%. is that doable?
[07:34] Priya Rao: yes canary and A/B are built in. you define percent rollout, and health checks include latency and failure rates plus your custom eval delta. automations can rollback if thresholds are breached.

[07:44] Maya Chen: ok time check — 15 minutes left. let's surface any blockers for the market listing itself.

[07:50] Nina Flores: blocking items: SOC2 docs, scheduled benchmark run, packaging manifest and helm chart, and finalizing pricing tier for hybrid listing (control plane hosted + runtime in VPC).

[07:59] Maya Chen: action items noted. Diego, let's discuss the benchmark plan — what you'll need from Argentum.

[08:04] Diego Alvarez: for a mini benchmark we need: sample traffic traces (qps distribution, token length histogram), model tarballs or model spec (size/arch), target regions, and a staging cluster (or permission to run on Redwood staging against the VPC runtime). we'll run a 1‑hour soak with multi‑slotted traffic and return p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and GPU utilization.
[08:25] Ravi Patel: we'll provide traces and a staging cluster. can you do 512-token window tests? we want to see memory behavior.
[08:31] Diego Alvarez: yes 512 and 2048 windows, we'll call out cache hit/miss rates.

[08:36] Omar Hassan: security: please include network drawing and list of inbound/outbound ports; include the trust cert rotation cadence.

[08:43] Priya Rao: will do — i'll attach the network diagram and cert rotation policy.

[08:48] Leah Kim: on the billing side, can we get a sample CSV with expected monthly spend scenarios? like baseline, peak, and burst?

[08:55] Maya Chen: yes i'll share a pricing workbook with three scenarios.

[09:00] Nina Flores: couple of small things — we'd like to test the fallback quality thresholds with our eval set before go‑live. can we stage that?

[09:06] Diego Alvarez: yes we can run the eval harness in your staging. recommend a small representative eval (200 prompts) for the initial gating.

[09:13] Ravi Patel: ok last question — marketplace terms: do you require exclusivity or minimum uptime commitments?

[09:19] Maya Chen: no exclusivity. uptime and SLA depend on listing mode — public hosted listings follow Redwood standard SLA; hybrid/private listings come under the enterprise contract where we can negotiate uptime and support SLAs.

[09:30] Nina Flores: great.

[09:33] Maya Chen: recap and next steps: 1) Maya to send marketplace packaging checklist and pricing workbook by 2025‑09‑05, 2) Diego to run mini benchmark once traces and staging cluster are provided (aim 2025‑09‑12 results), 3) Priya to share SOC2 attestation and KMS/integration docs, 4) Customer to grant staging access and provide traces by 2025‑09‑08.

[09:55] Ravi Patel: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:57] Omar Hassan: thanks, appreciate it.
[09:59] Maya Chen: thanks all — talk soon.

End of transcript
